1009.title: When the wind stopped
1009.hook: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun, and the wind god takes the breath out of the world
1009.carry: the breath is prana, the life in everything
1009.howItsDone: Many Hindus sit for a few slow breaths, pranayama, before puja or japa, treating the breath as prana, the life-force; some teachers shape the practice with Yoga Sutra 2.50's measures of place, time and number.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lion and the breath: steady breath, steady mind, learned from a guru.
screen: `THE LION AND THE BREATH.` · `LEARNED FROM A GURU.`

segments.voice: A baby wakes up hungry, sees the rising sun, red and round, and thinks it's a fruit. So he jumps for it. This baby is Hanuman, son of the wind, and his jump carries him high into the sky. Indra, king of the gods, sees a child rushing at the sun and strikes him with his thunderbolt. The baby falls onto a mountain, his jaw broken. And his father, Vayu, the wind, gathers him up, carries him into a cave, and stops moving.
screen: `A BABY JUMPS FOR THE SUN.` → `INDRA'S THUNDERBOLT.` → `THE WIND STOPS.`

segments.voice: This is from the Ramayana, told late in the epic by the sage Agastya. When the wind stops, everything stops with it. In the telling, no creature can breathe; bodies grow stiff as wood. The gods hurry to Brahma, and Brahma goes to the cave himself. He touches the child, and Hanuman comes back to life. The gods shower him with blessings, and a name sticks: Hanuman, from hanu, the jaw that was struck. Then Vayu moves again, and the whole world breathes. Here's the teaching under the story. In Hindu thought, breath isn't just air. It's prana, the life-force that moves through every living being. The Prashna Upanishad says everything rests on prana the way spokes rest in the hub of a wheel. Hanuman's story turns that into a picture: take away the wind, and nothing lives. That's why breath practice is a sacred practice in Hinduism, not only a way to relax. Pranayama means working with prana; ayama is a stretching, or a restraining. Patanjali's Yoga Sutra watches it closely: the breath going out, coming in and held still, each observed by place, by time and by number, until it grows long and subtle. So when someone in a Hindu home sits before puja and breathes slowly, they aren't only calming down. They're tending the gift the whole world went without, the day the wind stopped.
screen: `THE WIND STOPS. NOTHING BREATHES.` · `VAYU MOVES. THE WORLD BREATHES.` · `PRANA: THE HUB OF THE WHEEL.` · `PLACE, TIME, NUMBER: LONG AND SUBTLE.`

segments.voice: Sit the way you would before puja, or simply upright. Find where you feel the breath most, the nose, the chest or the belly, and count the in-breath and the out-breath until they're equal. Take six rounds on your fingers, and let only the time stretch, one count longer each way. When the rounds are done, let go of the counting; if you pray, give thanks for the breath, and if you don't, just notice it's been moving all along without your asking.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, why they're sacred: the breath is prana, the life Vayu gave back to the world, watched by place, time and number.
screen: `PRANAYAMA SEQUENCES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold on to it: the breath is prana, the life in everything. The day the wind stopped, so did the world. That's today, done.

1010.title: Nachiketa's chariot
1010.hook: a boy sent to Death waits three nights at the door, and Death teaches him with a chariot
1010.carry: atman is the rider, not the horses
1010.howItsDone: Some Hindus who keep a daily breath practice begin by choosing a clean, quiet spot and settling the body upright, in the order the Shvetashvatara Upanishad sets out, and hold the Katha Upanishad's picture of the self as the rider of the chariot.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the day the wind stopped: the breath is prana, the life in everything.
screen: `WHEN THE WIND STOPPED.` · `PRANA, THE LIFE IN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: A father is giving away his cows at a great sacrifice, and his young son Nachiketa notices they're old ones, past giving milk. So the boy asks: and to whom will you give me? He asks a second time. A third. And his father, fed up, snaps: to Death. The boy takes him at his word. He goes to the house of Yama, Death himself, and Yama isn't home. Nachiketa waits at the door for three nights, with nothing to eat.
screen: `TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?` → `TO DEATH.` → `THREE NIGHTS AT DEATH'S DOOR.`

segments.voice: This is the Katha Upanishad. Yama comes home, troubled that a guest has gone hungry, and offers three wishes, one for each night. For the third, the boy asks what everyone avoids: what happens to a person after death? Yama tries to buy him off. Take sons, gold, horses, a long life. Nachiketa says: keep your horses. So Death teaches him, and one of his pictures is a chariot. Know the self, the atman, as the one riding in the chariot. The body is the chariot. The intellect is the driver. The mind is the reins. The senses are the horses. Here's the big teaching: you are not your restless senses, and not even your racing mind. In the Upanishads the atman is the true self, the one who rides, and Yama says it is not born and does not die. When the driver is careless, the senses run wild like bad horses; when the driver understands and the reins are steady, the chariot reaches the end of the road. Another Upanishad, the Shvetashvatara, carries the chariot straight into breath practice: sit in a clean, level place out of the wind, hold the chest, neck and head upright, let the breath out gently through the nose, and hold the mind the way a driver holds restless horses. That's an order for a Hindu breath practice, read this way: place, body, breath, mind, so the rider can remember who's riding.
screen: `THREE WISHES. WHAT COMES AFTER DEATH?` · `KEEP YOUR HORSES. THE CHARIOT.` · `ATMAN: THE ONE WHO RIDES.` · `STEADY REINS, THE ROAD'S END.` · `PLACE, BODY, BREATH, MIND.`

segments.voice: Look at where you are, and move one thing that's in the way, a bag, a cup, a buzzing phone. Let the chest, neck and head stack upright, the chariot steady, and let each out-breath leave gently through the nose. When the mind pulls toward a sound or a worry, picture the reins and bring it back with a light hand; you're the one riding, not the horse that bolted.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the Upanishads' order and its reason: place, body, breath, mind, because the self, the atman, is the rider.

segments.voice: Hold on to it: atman is the rider, not the horses. Nachiketa turned down Death's horses to learn that. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1011.title: Arjuna's shaking hands
1011.hook: the finest archer in the army can't hold his bow, and Krishna's answer reaches down to the breath
1011.carry: samatva: evenness in success and failure is yoga
1011.howItsDone: Some Hindus who practice pranayama close with a few rounds of even breathing, a practice teachers connect with Gita 5.27; many also offer the result of their work to God, the karma yoga of Gita 2.47–2.48.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nachiketa at Death's door, and Yama's chariot: atman is the rider, not the horses.
screen: `NACHIKETA'S CHARIOT.` · `ATMAN IS THE RIDER.`

segments.voice: Two armies face each other on the field of Kurukshetra, conch shells blaring. Arjuna, the finest archer on either side, asks his charioteer, Krishna, to drive him out between them so he can see who he's fighting. He sees teachers. Uncles. Cousins. And his body gives out. His limbs go weak, his mouth goes dry, his skin burns, his hair stands on end, and his great bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand. He can't stand. He sits down in the chariot.
screen: `TWO ARMIES, CONCHES BLARING.` → `HE SEES HIS OWN FAMILY.` → `THE BOW SLIPS FROM HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: That's how the Bhagavad Gita begins: not with a calm sage, but with a body in panic. Yesterday's picture comes alive here: a chariot, a driver, and a rider who has forgotten who he is. Krishna's teaching meets him there. In the second chapter he gives it a name. Your right is to the action, never to its fruits. So do the work, without clinging, the same in success and in failure. Evenness, samatva, is called yoga. It runs through the whole Gita: even in pleasure and pain, even toward friend and foe. And it reaches all the way down to the body. In the fifth chapter, Krishna describes the sage at practice: the outside world shut out, the gaze resting between the brows, the in-breath and the out-breath made even as they move within the nostrils, free of desire, fear and anger. Many teachers read the two passages together: Arjuna's body shook because his mind was torn over what the battle would cost, and Krishna's answer is an even mind, with an even breath traveling with it. This is the heart of what Hindus call karma yoga: you do your dharma, your rightful work, fully, and you offer the result instead of clutching it. If everything hangs on the result, the hands shake. If the result is offered, the breath can settle. So the breath practice of these days ends here: the breath honored as prana, the rider in the chariot, and now in and out made even, because the one breathing has let go of the outcome.
screen: `THE ACTION IS YOURS, NOT THE FRUIT.` · `SAMATVA: EVENNESS IS YOGA.` · `IN-BREATH AND OUT-BREATH MADE EVEN.` · `KARMA YOGA: DO THE WORK, OFFER THE RESULT.`

segments.voice: With place and body settled, let the breath swing a little for a few rounds, a slightly longer out-breath, then a slightly longer in-breath. Then let them meet, in for four and out for four, quiet within the nostrils. When it's steady, bring to mind one thing waiting for you today, and offer how it turns out, in a prayer if you pray, or just by loosening your grip on it; then see if the breath stays level on its own.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, where the Gita lets them rest: in-breath and out-breath made even, an even breath for an even mind.
screen: `PRANAYAMA SEQUENCES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold on to it: samatva, evenness in success and failure is yoga. Arjuna's bow slipped, and Krishna began right there. Until tomorrow.

1012.title: Holding the wind
1012.hook: Arjuna says holding the mind still is like holding the wind; Krishna doesn't disagree
1012.carry: practice and letting go hold the restless mind
1012.howItsDone: Hindus who undertake a mantra sadhana may begin with a sankalpa, a resolve naming the mantra, the time, the place and the span, and then keep the practice daily, sometimes with a teacher's guidance.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences ended with Arjuna's shaking hands: samatva, evenness in success and failure, is yoga.
screen: `ARJUNA'S SHAKING HANDS.` · `EVENNESS IS YOGA.`

segments.voice: The mind is restless, Arjuna says. Turbulent, strong, stubborn. Trying to hold it still, he tells Krishna, seems as hard as holding the wind. It's the sixth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, and Krishna has just described a yogi sitting in perfect steadiness, like a lamp in a windless place. Arjuna's answer is blunt: that sounds lovely, and I can't see how it could last. What's striking is Krishna's reply. He doesn't tell Arjuna he's wrong. He agrees. Then he names the two things that work anyway.
screen: `THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA AGREES.` → `THEN HE NAMES WHAT WORKS.`

segments.voice: Gita six, verse thirty-five, in paraphrase: without doubt the mind is restless and hard to hold, but it can be held by practice and by letting go. Practice is abhyasa, steady repeated effort. Letting go is vairagya, loosening the grip of wanting. That pair is a core Hindu teaching on the mind. Hold on to the first: again and again. That's the ground this new block stands on. Its name has two words. Mantra: a sacred sound or phrase, a syllable like Om, a name of God, a line from a text. Sadhana: a practice kept as a discipline, done regularly with a purpose. Together, a mantra returned to on purpose, not said once when the mood is right. The block's title adds japa, repetition, and a span, forty days. Tradition gives spans like that; the verses here don't fix a number, and the coming days look at that. Where does a sadhana begin? In some lineages, with a sankalpa, a resolve said or held at the start. It sets the terms before the effort: which mantra, at what time, where, how long. A sankalpa isn't a mood. It's closer to a promise with the details written in. Here's why that matters, given Arjuna's wind. A restless mind is very good at renegotiating. Later? Shorter today? A different mantra? The sankalpa settles those questions once, at the start, so the mind has less to argue with each morning. Krishna's answer was practice. The sankalpa is how practice gets a shape.
screen: `HELD BY PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.` · `MANTRA: A SACRED SOUND OR PHRASE.` · `SADHANA: A PRACTICE KEPT AS DISCIPLINE.` · `SANKALPA: SET THE TERMS AT THE START.`

segments.voice: Settle the place, the body and a few gentle breaths, the way the pranayama days ended. Without saying any mantra yet, set the terms of a small sadhana: a mantra from your own tradition if you pray, or Om, or a single word that matters to you; a time; a place; and a length small enough to keep. Hold those four clearly, like words on a card, then let them go and sit with the breath.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline, returned to on purpose. It begins with practice, abhyasa, and in some lineages with a sankalpa that sets the terms.

1013.title: Beads from Shiva's tears
1013.hook: Shiva opens his eyes after a long meditation, and his tears become the seeds of a mala
1013.carry: all things strung on God, like mala beads
1013.howItsDone: Hindus who keep japa may count on a mala, a string of beads of tulsi wood, rudraksha or other materials, moving one bead per repetition and turning the string at the larger meru bead rather than crossing it.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna said the mind is like the wind, and Krishna agreed: practice and letting go hold the restless mind.
screen: `HOLDING THE WIND.` · `PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana, Shiva sits in meditation for a thousand years of the gods. When at last he opens his eyes, tears fall from them to the earth. Where they land, trees grow, and their seeds are called rudraksha: Rudra's eye, Rudra being a name of Shiva. Dark, knobbly seeds, with lines running down their sides. Devotees of Shiva string them into a mala, and many wear one, or count a mantra on it, every day.
screen: `SHIVA OPENS HIS EYES.` → `HIS TEARS FALL.` → `THEY GROW INTO RUDRAKSHA.`

segments.voice: Mala means a garland, the same word as flowers placed around a neck or on an image of God. A japa mala is a garland for counting a mantra. Devotees of Shiva favor rudraksha; devotees of Vishnu and Krishna favor tulsi wood, from the holy basil many families tend at home. One bead is larger and sits apart, with a tassel: the meru, sharing its name with the sacred mountain at the center of the world. Teachers in several lineages say not to cross it; at the end of a round, you turn the string and go back. Their reasons vary. Some say the meru stands for the guru or for God, and you don't step over what you honor. Others say turning back keeps each round awake. Now the teaching the beads carry. In the Gita's seventh chapter, Krishna says all of this world is strung on him, like gems on a thread. The beads are what you see; the thread holding them is hidden. That's a central Hindu teaching: the many things of the world aren't scattered. One divine reality runs through them all, the way one cord runs through every bead. And in the sixth chapter Krishna says, wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back. The bead is that return, made into something your thumb can feel. The mind drifts to a bill or a text; the thumb moves to the next bead; you're back on the thread. Shiva's seeds or Vishnu's basil, the mala teaches with your hands: many beads, one thread.

Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, the tool in the hand: the mala, its meru, and the one thread running through every bead.

1014.title: Narada asks for the rules
1014.hook: who gets to hand you a mantra? the tradition gives more than one answer, and keeps them all
1014.carry: a mantra is received, not invented
1014.howItsDone: In some Hindu lineages a mantra is received privately from a guru at diksha, initiation; in others, such as the public chanting of the divine names, the mantra is open to anyone who wants to say it.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOURTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, beads from Shiva's tears: all things strung on God, like mala beads.
screen: `BEADS FROM SHIVA'S TEARS.` · `ALL STRUNG ON ONE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Who gets to hand you a mantra? In one family, a grandfather leans close to a teenager's ear at a ceremony and whispers a line meant for that ear alone, never to be said aloud to friends. In a park across town, a group sits in a circle singing names of God loud enough for joggers to hear, and anyone who wants to sit down is welcome to join. Both are mantra. Both are japa, in a way. And both have scripture behind them.
screen: `A LINE WHISPERED INTO ONE EAR.` → `NAMES SUNG IN A PARK.` → `BOTH HAVE SCRIPTURE BEHIND THEM.`

segments.voice: Start with the whisper. In some lineages, a mantra is received from a guru at diksha, initiation. The teacher chooses it and gives it, and the student keeps it private. The idea is that a mantra given this way carries the teacher's blessing and the lineage's practice behind it; there, picking one off a website isn't the same thing at all. Now the park. In a short text called the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, the sage Narada asks the god Brahma how to get through the hard age the tradition calls the Kali Yuga. Brahma answers with a mantra made of the names Hare, Rama and Krishna. Narada asks the obvious follow-up: what are the rules? And Brahma says there are none. Say it, and that's enough. Some communities point to that line for their open, public chanting. Then there's Om. In the Katha Upanishad, Death himself teaches a boy named Nachiketa that the word all the Vedas point to, the word sought by those who live in discipline, is Om. And some mantras are drawn from the old texts, like Om namah shivaya, honoring Shiva, whose words namah shivaya appear in the Shri Rudram. So how does someone choose? It depends on the path. But here's what every answer shares, and it's a real Hindu teaching: a mantra is received, not invented. The Vedas themselves are called shruti, what was heard, by seers who received them. A guru passes a mantra on; Brahma gives the names to Narada for everyone. Whichever you receive, the sadhana is to stay with it.
screen: `DIKSHA: A MANTRA GIVEN BY A GURU.` · `NARADA ASKS THE RULES: THERE ARE NONE.` · `OM: THE WORD THE VEDAS POINT TO.` · `SHRUTI: WHAT WAS HEARD.` · `RECEIVED, NOT INVENTED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the mantra you chose two days ago, or Om if you haven't chosen, and notice where it came from: a teacher, a family, a text, a temple, a song. Then begin the japa, silently or in a whisper, one repetition per breath or per bead. If another mantra drifts in, let it pass and come back to the one you chose; staying with one is the practice.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, where the mantra comes from: a guru's diksha, the names given for all, or the word the Vedas point to. Received, not invented.

segments.voice: Hold on to it: a mantra is received, not invented. A whisper or a park, each one arrives from somewhere. Rest well.

1015.title: The seer of the Gayatri
1015.hook: a king loses to a sage's staff, becomes a seer himself, and the verse prayed at dawn and dusk is credited to him
1015.carry: sandhya: prayer at the joints of the day

1015.howItsDone: Many Hindu families keep sandhya, a rite at dawn and dusk built around the Gayatri, credited to the seer Vishvamitra; some who keep a mantra sadhana tie their own japa to those same hinges of the day.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Narada asks for the rules: a mantra is received, not invented.
screen: `NARADA ASKS FOR THE RULES.` · `RECEIVED, NOT INVENTED.`

segments.voice: A king named Vishvamitra rides with his army into a forest hermitage and sees the sage Vasishtha's wonderful cow, the one who can give anything. He wants her. He offers thousands of cows, elephants, gold. Vasishtha won't part with her. The king tries to take her by force, and she brings forth armies that rout his. He goes off and wins divine weapons by austerity, comes back, and turns them on the sage himself, and every one is swallowed by a single thing: Vasishtha's wooden staff. The king looks at his empty hands and says: shame on a warrior's strength; a sage's strength is the real strength.
screen: `A KING WANTS THE SAGE'S COW.` → `EVERY WEAPON SWALLOWED BY A STAFF.` → `A SAGE'S STRENGTH IS REAL STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: That's the Ramayana, in its first book. The king sets down his crown and begins tapas, a long austerity that runs, in the telling, thousands of years, through failures, temper and temptation, until Vasishtha himself calls him a brahmarshi, a sage of the highest rank. And to this seer the tradition credits one of the most loved verses in Hinduism. It's in the third book of the Rig Veda, the book of Vishvamitra's family, and it's called the Gayatri, or the Savitri, after Savitr, the divine sun who stirs the world awake. Its prayer, in paraphrase: we meditate on the bright glory of the divine sun; may it stir our minds. Not a prayer for a win, or a crop, or a kingdom. For understanding. A king who learned his weapons were nothing next to a sage's insight gives the world a prayer for light in the mind. Here's the practice built around it. The Manusmriti, one of the old books of dharma, says: at dawn, stand repeating the Savitri until the sun is seen; at dusk, sit repeating it until the stars appear. The joints of the day are called sandhya, a joining, and the rite kept at them is called sandhya too. In many families it's tied to the sacred-thread initiation, and the verse is learned from a teacher. But anyone can see what the timing teaches: prayer belongs at the hinges, where night turns to day and day to night. The light itself keeps the time.
screen: `THE KING BECOMES A SEER.` · `THE GAYATRI: MAY IT STIR OUR MINDS.` · `STAND AT DAWN, SIT AT DUSK.` · `SANDHYA: THE JOINTS OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Notice the light where you are right now, morning, afternoon or evening, then begin your own mantra, silently or in a whisper, and let it run. As it runs, choose your hinge, the first light or the last, where the mantra will start tomorrow: when the light changes, not when a free moment turns up.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, its when: the sandhya, the joints of the day, where Vishvamitra's verse is kept at dawn and dusk.
